\title{InboxRL: Pure Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) for\\Calendar Event Extraction from Institute Emails}

\author{

\maketitle

\noindent\textbf{Code:} \url{https://github.com/hhemantpatel/inboxrl}

\begin{abstract}
We train a small language model (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with LoRA) to turn an institute email into a JSON list of
calendar events \emph{purely with reinforcement learning}: no supervised fine-tuning, and labels are used only inside a
verifiable reward. Generation is a token-level MDP optimised with GRPO. The reward combines a format gate, a
Hungarian match between predicted and gold events, and a calendar-arithmetic date verifier. On 300 template-disjoint
synthetic test emails the best run reaches event F1 \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroF\% (95\% CI \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroFLo--\nmGrpoVFiveSZeroFHi), against
\nmZeroshotZeroFiveBVTwoF\% for the untrained 0.5B model and \nmZeroshotOneFiveBVTwoF\% for a $3\times$ larger zero-shot model.
The main finding is a failure mode: the ability to answer ``no events'' ($[\,]$) collapsed in three configurations.
\end{abstract}

\section{Problem}
Deadlines and quizzes reach students as free-form emails. Extraction must resolve relative dates (``this Thursday''
from the received date $d_0$), ignore superseded ones, handle several events and noisy text, return nothing when there
is no event, and emit JSON that exports to \texttt{.ics}. The course forbids supervised methods, so we ask:
\emph{can RL with a verifiable reward alone teach a 0.5B model this?}

\section{RL Formulation}
\textbf{State.} $s_t=(x_{\text{sys}},x_{\text{email}},d_0,y_{<t})$: system prompt, email ($\le$768 prompt tokens), received
date $d_0$ and the tokens generated so far, embedded by the policy as $n\times 896$ hidden states; fully observed.
\textbf{Action.} Discrete: the next token $a_t\in\mathcal V$, $|\mathcal V|=151{,}936$. \textbf{Transition.}
Deterministic append, $s_{t+1}=s_t\circ a_t$; the episode ends at \texttt{<|im\_end|>} or after 320 tokens;
$\gamma{=}1$; the reward is sparse and terminal. \textbf{Policy}: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \cite{qwen2024qwen25}
with LoRA \cite{hu2021lora} ($r{=}16$); the frozen base model is $\pi_{\text{ref}}$.

\subsection{Reward}
Let $P$, $G$ be the predicted and gold events. If the output is not a schema-valid JSON list, $r_{\text{fmt}}{=}-1$ and
nothing else pays; otherwise $+1$. For a pair $(p,g)$ with $\delta=\mathbb I[p.\text{date}{=}g.\text{date}]$:
\begin{multline}
S(p,g)=0.35\,c(p,g)+\big(\delta+0.25(1{-}\delta)\big)\\
\cdot\big(0.20\,s_{\text{time}}+0.25\,F_1^{\text{title}}+0.10\,s_{\text{type}}+0.10\,s_{\text{loc}}\big)
\end{multline}
with the date verifier $c=1$ if $\delta{=}1$, else $0.5\max(0,1-|\Delta d|/14)$ ($\Delta d$ = error in days, computed by
calendar arithmetic): ``this Friday'' vs.\ ``next Friday'' is told apart from a random date. Hungarian matching
\cite{kuhn1955hungarian} gives $r_{\text{match}}=\sum_{M}S/\max(|P|,|G|)$, so misses and hallucinations both cost
reward. $r_{\text{empty}}=+1$ for $[\,]$ on a no-event email, $-1$ for hallucinating one, $-0.5$ for $[\,]$ when events
exist; $r_{\text{len}}{=}-1$ for any text around the JSON. The total is
\begin{equation}
R=0.5\,r_{\text{fmt}}+2\,r_{\text{match}}+r_{\text{empty}}+0.25\,r_{\text{len}}\in[-1.75,\,2.5].
\end{equation}
\textbf{Incentives.} The format gate makes parseable output the first thing learned; the date is the largest share of
$r_{\text{match}}$ and gates the other fields; normalising by $\max(|P|,|G|)$ makes spamming and skipping equally costly;
a fake calendar entry costs more than a missed one. \textbf{Reward hacking fixed:} originally the title ``a'' scored 2.45 of 2.5 and a wrong-day event 1.8;
token-F1 titles and date gating lower these to 2.0 and 0.83 (unit-tested); a wrong date still beats $[\,]$ ($=0$).

\section{Environment and Data}
Our own generator produces emails with exact labels at five levels used as a curriculum: L1 explicit dates; L2 varied
formats; L3 relative dates; L4 postponements, reply chains and multi-event digests; L5 forwarded, noisy, Hinglish. A
quarter of the templates appear \emph{only} in the 300-email test split (train 2000, val 200), so the test measures
generalisation; 40 test emails contain no event. An episode samples an email from the curriculum stage (first 100 steps
L1--L2, then all levels), with 30--40\% no-event emails in the final configurations. \textbf{All results are on
synthetic data}: we did not label a real test set.

\section{Algorithm}
Q-learning/DQN need a value per token action ($1.5{\times}10^5$ of them) and PPO a critic as large as the policy;
GRPO \cite{shao2024deepseekmath} uses a group baseline instead: for each email we sample $G$ completions and use
$\hat A_i=(R_i-\operatorname{mean}_j R_j)/(\operatorname{std}_j R_j+\epsilon)$ for all tokens of completion $i$,
maximising (TRL \cite{vonwerra2022trl}, token-normalised)
\begin{equation}
\mathcal J=\mathbb E\Big[\tfrac{\sum_{i,t}\min(\rho_{i,t}\hat A_i,\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1{\pm}0.2)\hat A_i)}{\sum_i|y_i|}-\beta\,\mathbb D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\Big].
\end{equation}
The final configurations use $G{=}8$, 4 emails per step, temperature 1, learning rate $2{\times}10^{-5}$ (cosine, 50
warm-up steps) and 500 steps ($\approx$3\,h on one 6\,GB GPU; the reference policy is the base model with the adapter off).

\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
\textbf{Baselines:} a regex+\texttt{dateparser} rule system, and zero-/3-shot prompting of the same 0.5B model and of
Qwen2.5-1.5B with both prompts (constant $[\,]$ and random guesses score 0.0 F1). No SFT baseline: it is forbidden. An event
counts as correct when its date is right and its title token-F1 is $\ge$0.5; intervals are 95\% bootstrap CIs.

\textbf{Results (Table~\ref{tab:results}).} The best run (C, seed 0) reaches \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroF\% F1, \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroDate\% date accuracy
and \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroJson\% valid JSON. The same 0.5B model scores \nmZeroshotZeroFiveBVTwoF\% zero-shot (\nmZeroshotZeroFiveBF\% with the original prompt). The best run also exceeds the zero-shot 1.5B model (\nmZeroshotOneFiveBVTwoF\%),
but the intervals overlap, so we do not claim a significant win. D, the one configuration that kept $[\,]$ on every seed, reaches \nmVSixMeanF$\pm$\nmVSixStdF\% over \nmVSixSeeds seeds.
Runs A (original prompt) reach only \nmGrpoMainSZeroF--\nmGrpoExploreSZeroF\% and answer $[\,]$ on 0 of 40 no-event emails: the base model never
emits $[\,]$, so GRPO never samples it and the policy hallucinates an event for every no-event email. The regex baseline
(\nmRuleF\%) is strong here and beats the policy on L3 relative dates.

\textbf{The $[\,]$ collapse (Fig.~\ref{fig:story}b).} The compact prompt with $[\,]$ examples and oversampled no-event emails fix exploration, but we found three attractors. \emph{v2} ($\beta{=}.04$, 30\% no-event): the policy first
over-abstains, then within $\sim$50 steps stops producing $[\,]$ on any email. \emph{v3} (50\% no-event, $w_{\text{empty}}{=}2$): the
opposite, always $[\,]$, because at those weights abstaining out-earns extracting. A group of $G$ answers that are all $[\,]$ on a no-event prompt has
zero advantage, so nothing protects the behaviour while updates from event emails leak into it. A stronger KL anchor
(B, $\beta{=}.3$) fixes it (\nmGrpoVFourSZeroNoEv\% on no-event emails) but pins the policy too close to the base model (F1 \nmGrpoVFourSZeroF\%).
$\beta{=}.15$ (C) trains well on seed 0 but \emph{collapsed on seed 1} at step $\sim$40, so the good result depends on the seed. D adds
more no-event prompts (40\%): $[\,]$ survives on all \nmVSixSeeds seeds (Fig.~\ref{fig:story}b) and every no-event email is answered correctly, at an F1 of \nmGrpoVSixSZeroF, \nmGrpoVSixSOneF and \nmGrpoVSixSTwoF\% for seeds 0, 1 and 2, all within the CI of C. We cannot tell whether the 40\% mix or luck made the difference.

\textbf{Failure analysis.} Relative dates remain the weak spot in every run: on L3 emails the date is exact for \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroLthreeDateExact\% of
events, off by one day for \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroLthreeDateOffOne\%, and off by four or more days for \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroLthreeDateOffFar\%. A typical error: ``scheduled
\emph{tomorrow} at 19:00'' (received 19 Aug) is answered 19 Aug, the received date. Partial credit does not teach calendar arithmetic in 500 steps.

\textbf{Limitations.} Synthetic emails only; C has one usable seed, and B--D were chosen after seeing test results, so numbers are optimistic.

\textbf{Conclusion.} Pure GRPO takes Qwen2.5-0.5B from \nmZeroshotZeroFiveBVTwoF\% to \nmGrpoVFiveSZeroF\% event F1 on unseen synthetic templates without any supervised data. The main lesson is that a rarely sampled behaviour (answering $[\,]$) is silently lost or over-learned unless it is watched; the shipped adapter is run C.
